clue.text: Just as orgasm prompts poem by Yeats … (3,6,6)

blocks.note: 'The second she walked in' and 'just as she walked in' are the same sentence — the phrase works as a conjunction meaning the very moment
the vulgar verb for reaching a climax, in its -ing form

explanation.surface: An orgasm putting somebody in mind of a bit of Irish poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Yeats wrote it in 1919 — 'Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold' — and took the title from the promised return of Christ, which is the sense the setter is quietly swapping for a cruder one. The dots run the sentence on into 9 across.
explanation.definitionFit: The Second Coming is Yeats's best-known poem, so the definition names the answer by its title rather than by any meaning of the words.

clue.text: Backup part of database liable to corruption (9)

blocks.note: an office short of hands brings in a temp for backup, someone standing in for a while
a database is built out of tables, one for each kind of record

explanation.surface: A spare copy of some data sitting where it could easily be damaged.
explanation.walkthrough: A temp table is a genuine database object, so the first two thirds of the clue read as one technical phrase and give no hint that they are two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody temptable can be led astray, so the corruption meant is the moral kind — being bought — and not data going bad.

clue.text: Sea-sick seabird from China? (7)

indicators.note: Something sick is out of sorts and not itself, so the three letters beside it will not stand in the order they were given.

blocks.note: the three letters of SEA, no longer in that order
a tern is the slender gull-like seabird, and one of the crossword's regulars

explanation.surface: A queasy seabird that has flown in from China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sea-sick' looks like one word describing the bird, and the hyphen is where the fodder ends and its instruction begins. The question mark earns its place: China is one eastern country among many.
explanation.definitionFit: China lies in the East, so 'from China?' defines by example — one eastern country asked to stand in for the adjective itself.

clue.text: Challenging former lover on stage (8)

blocks.note: your ex is the partner you used to have
what a person up on the stage is doing

explanation.surface: An old flame being difficult up on the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Challenging' looks like the verb, somebody squaring up to their ex, and it is the adjective — the sense in which a job or a boss makes demands you can barely meet.
explanation.definitionFit: An exacting employer demands a great deal and accepts nothing less, which is 'challenging' in its adjectival, hard-to-satisfy sense.

clue.text: Huge honour to sit on banks of Seine (5)

indicators.note: This entry runs down the grid, so whatever sits on another thing is written above it.
A river's banks are its two edges, so the letters wanted are the ones at either end of the word with nothing from between.

blocks.note: the OBE, Officer of the Order of the British Empire, is a rank of honour handed out twice a year in Britain
the first and last letters of Seine, the two edges of the word

explanation.surface: A grand award being presented on a Paris riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Huge honour' hangs together as a phrase — the sort of thing a recipient says on the day — and only the first word is the definition, describing a body rather than an award.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese is the medical adjective for grossly overweight, so 'Huge' is the everyday word for the same bulk.

clue.text: Re-entering language course (9)

indicators.note: What enters a thing ends up inside it, so these two letters are planted within the word named next.

blocks.note: diction is a speaker's language, the words chosen and the way they are delivered
the clue's own opening syllable, its two letters taken just as they are printed

explanation.surface: Going back into a language class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Re-entering' reads as a single word meaning going back in, and the hyphen is the seam: the prefix is letters and everything after it is instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship or a career holds a course, which is the direction it is set on, so the two nouns swap straight over.

clue.text: Gone wild with axes splitting something needed for fire (6)

indicators.note: Something gone wild is beyond all control, and letters in that state keep none of the order they arrived in.
To split a thing is to open a gap in the middle of it, and that gap is where the next piece goes.

blocks.note: the four letters of GONE in a new order, then prised apart after the first
the x and y axes of a graph

explanation.surface: Someone rampaging with axes through the wood for the fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Axes' is the plural of axis, not of axe, and that single swap is what keeps the woodpile in front of you when the wordplay is really drawing a graph.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire cannot burn without oxygen, so the definition names it by the job it does in combustion rather than by any synonym.

clue.text: Provide detailed account of quite miserable passage (7)

indicators.note: A passage is a way running straight through something, and the letters wanted run straight through the two words in front of it.

blocks.note: seven letters in a row, starting two into the first word and stopping four into the second

explanation.surface: A rather gloomy stretch of writing being gone through line by line.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden runs are hardest to see across a word break, and 'passage' passes for part of the description — a miserable passage of prose — while doing the work of the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To itemise is to set a thing out item by item, which is what providing a detailed account of something amounts to.

clue.text: Donates, as replacing 4, 6 and 15 (5)

indicators.note: One thing replacing another takes its place exactly: the letters named move out and the letters beside the instruction move in.

blocks.note: to donate is to give, and the clue's tense makes it the third person
the Roman numeral for four, and it is sitting in the middle of the previous word
the small word of the surface, handed over as two letters to fill the gap

explanation.surface: A donor's gifts standing in for three items further up the list.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers do two different jobs in one short clue: 4 is Roman numerals inside a word, while 6 and 15 are grid references pointing at other answers.
explanation.definitionFit: 6 down is OXYGEN and 15 across is NEON, so the definition names them by the class both of them belong to.

clue.text: … wrongly read note by misfortunate Keats (7)

indicators.note: A name that has come off badly has been knocked out of shape, so its letters do not keep the order they were printed in.

blocks.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale, after do and re
the five letters of the poet's name, dealt out in another order

explanation.surface: Somebody misreading a note left by a luckless Keats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' wants to be the thing that was misread and it is the sol-fa syllable. The dots carry the sentence on from 1 across, where a poet's name was doing a completely different job.
explanation.definitionFit: To mistake something is to take it wrongly — to read a remark or a signal the wrong way — which is what the definition describes.

clue.text: For example, Keats and Yeats (or not) (7)

definitions.text: For example, Keats and Yeats (or not)

blocks.note: two poets offered as instances of something, and on the page the names look like a matched pair, one letter apart
the bracket takes the pairing back: one name is said 'keets' and the other 'yates', so they look alike and do not sound alike

explanation.surface: Two famous poets put forward as an example of something, with a bracketed second thought.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to hunt for here. Both men wrote verse, so both qualify — but only as poets, never as a matching pair, which is what the aside owns up to.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhymer is a writer of verse, and both men are instances of the class — though their names are the one pair that will not rhyme.

clue.text: See 25
Heretics are punished for unfaithful acts (11)

indicators.note: A word under punishment is being knocked about, and letters knocked about do not stay in the order they arrived in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: Heretics being punished for breaking faith.
explanation.walkthrough: Surface and answer are about the same thing, which is what makes the letters so hard to see: breaking faith is precisely what heretics were burned for.
explanation.definitionFit: A treachery is an act of betrayal, a broken faith with somebody who trusted you, and the plural definition matches the plural answer.

clue.text: You might slip on this bats blood (6,4)

blocks.note: both words are slang for crazy — he's gone completely bats, he's gone completely bananas
your blood is your kin, the family you are related to

explanation.surface: A witch's recipe of bats' blood, and a warning not to tread in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole first half and works by what the thing does to you. In British political talk the same phrase names any small object that trips a career up.
explanation.definitionFit: A banana skin left on the pavement is the classic thing to slip on, so the definition describes the answer by what happens when you tread on it.

clue.text: International waters still surrounded by dumb-asses (5,4)

indicators.note: Dumb here is the American sense, stupid rather than silent, and a word made stupid loses whatever sense its order gave it.
What surrounds a thing closes round it on both sides, so this piece ends up inside the letters named after it.

blocks.note: the five letters of ASSES re-sorted, then opened up after the first to take something in
still in the sense of 'still better' — swap in 'even better' and the phrase is unchanged

explanation.surface: A stretch of calm water with fools standing all round it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like a description of the water and means even. The seven seas is the old sailors' phrase for all the oceans there are, which is why one country cannot own them.
explanation.definitionFit: The seven seas are the world's oceans taken together, the waters no nation owns, so the definition names them by their legal standing.

clue.text: Light’s non-binding energy (4)

indicators.note: Binding goes round and round a thing, so the word in front of it closes over the letter that comes next.

blocks.note: the three letters at the front of the hyphenated word, taken as they stand
e = energy, the E of Einstein's equation

explanation.surface: A lamp's energy, offered with no commitment attached.
explanation.walkthrough: The chemistry is real: neon is a noble gas and bonds with nothing, so 'non-binding' describes the answer at the same time as it hides the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A neon is the glowing tube itself in everyday speech, so 'Light' names the answer by the thing the gas is bought for.

clue.text: Dropping dead, wrote frantically (6,3)

indicators.note: Writing done frantically comes out in a scramble, so the letters beside it land in no particular order.

blocks.note: a dead leg is a numb one, with no feeling left in it
the five letters of WROTE, scribbled down in another order

explanation.surface: Somebody dropping dead after a frantic bout of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dropping' is a noun and not the verb the surface offers — the sort of thing a bird leaves on a car roof — and the answer is the nursery euphemism for the same article.
explanation.definitionFit: A dropping is a piece of excrement and number two is the nursery word for it, so the two nouns name one thing at different levels of politeness.

clue.text: Fresher report of any toilet more sullied (8)

indicators.note: A report of something is that thing as it was heard, so what follows is judged by ear and written down however the sound allows.

WC = water closet, the label on a lavatory door
the four letters of MORE, put back in a different order

explanation.surface: A student's account of a lavatory that has got dirtier.
explanation.walkthrough: Spelling a word out of letter names — enn, ee — is the step to spot, and it hides because 'report of any' reads as ordinary reporting. In Britain a fresher is a first-year university student.
explanation.definitionFit: A fresher has just arrived and knows nobody, so the definition works by example: one particular kind of newcomer standing for all of them.

blocks.note: the NATO alphabet gives this letter a whole word to say over the radio, so the capital on its own is four letters
no letters from this one: it is the same character again, smaller and a moment later, and the printed dots are the pause in between

explanation.walkthrough: Any repeated letter would draw a picture of the thing; only this one also names it, because the radio alphabet turns E into a word. That is why the four-letter enumeration is fair.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue prints a letter, a pause, then the same letter fainter — which is what an echo is, a sound coming back quieter than it went out.

clue.text: Take end from communion wafer – on reflection, an exaltation! (7)

the small word of the surface, handed straight over as it stands
those same two letters shown in a mirror, so they come back the other way round

explanation.walkthrough: One tiny word does the job twice, forwards and then mirrored, which is the whole difficulty of the second half. Hosanna is the cry the crowd raised on Palm Sunday.
explanation.definitionFit: A hosanna is a shout of praise to God, and an exaltation is exactly that: the lifting of something high in worship.

clue.text: Slight temperature dropping off with cool hormone (7)

explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' looks like an adjective attached to the temperature and it is a noun meaning a snub — two words that read as one symptom are two separate pieces.

clue.text: A right-beginning, dotted-letter-including alphabet (6)

clue.text: Gordon’s starter presented to massive foody? (11)

clue.text: Sadness as building terminally fire-damaged (5)

clue.text: That man follows backwash of river froth (6)

clue.text: Playing bingo, the French are mean (7)
